evidence.quote: On completion of a request, the final response is written to idem:resp:{idempotency_key} with a 24-hour TTL.
on a hit, it returns the stored response immediately without touching DynamoDB or the Orchestrator
merchants frequently use their own order or invoice identifiers, which is accepted
A Redis key without merchant_id, read before any hash check, lets one merchant's request match another merchant's stored response, and lets a changed body return a stale response instead of 422.

reassessment.note: Version 1.1 fixed the DynamoDB key only. Section 9.2 and the Section 24 decision still use idem:resp:{key}.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 9.2 and in the Section 24 Idempotency store row, change the key to idem:resp:{merchant_id}:{idempotency_key}. Store request_hash with the cached response and return it only when the hashes match. On a mismatch, return 422 (or fall through to DynamoDB).
recommendation.expected_benefit: Restores FR-5 and P3, and removes cross-merchant response disclosure.
recommendation.issue: The fast-path key leaves out the merchant, and a hit bypasses the request-hash comparison.
recommendation.rationale: P3 scopes idempotency to (merchant, key), and FR-5 requires HTTP 422 on a body mismatch; the fast path currently enforces neither.
recommendation.verification: Add to the FR-5 test: two merchants send the same key with different bodies and each gets its own payment; one merchant resends a key with a modified body while the Redis entry is warm and gets 422.

findings.statement: Version 1.1 changed the DynamoDB key to merchant_id#idempotency_key but left the Redis fast path at idem:resp:{idempotency_key}. A cache hit returns the stored response without reaching DynamoDB. Section 9.1 accepts merchants' own order and invoice numbers as keys, so two merchants can easily use the same key. Merchant B could then receive merchant A's payment object while its own payment is never created. A reused key with a different body would get the old response instead of the HTTP 422 that FR-5 requires. This breaks P3 and FR-5 and discloses data across merchants.
findings.title: Redis idempotency fast path is still keyed without the merchant and skips the body-hash check

evidence.quote: exactly one request can acquire the lock for a given merchant and key regardless of which region receives it
using the default multi-Region eventual consistency mode. The Payments API in each region reads and writes its local replica.
so a merchant retry that Route 53 sends to the Jakarta cell during a failover or a partial Singapore outage is deduplicated against the original request

With eventual consistency and region-local writes, a conditional put in one region is checked only against that region's replica, so two regions can each succeed within the replication lag — exactly the partial-outage window the design relies on.

next_step.action: Choose the lock-authority model and confirm the replication-mode semantics before Phase 3 build of the idempotency layer.

reassessment.note: Introduced by the 1.1 change to a writable DynamoDB global table and the Jakarta warm cell.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 9.4, choose one of two fixes. (a) Make Singapore the single lock authority: Jakarta forwards idempotency lock acquisition to Singapore while Singapore is reachable, and takes local locks only after a declared failover that fences the Singapore cells. (b) Move to a strongly consistent multi-region mode, if the platform team confirms one is available in these regions. Remove the 'exactly one request ... regardless of which region' claim until one of these is in place, and update the Section 24 'both writable' wording to match.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Keeps FR-5 at-most-one authorization during failover and partial outages, which is when merchant retry storms are most likely.
recommendation.issue: The design relies on cross-region mutual exclusion that its chosen replication mode cannot provide.
recommendation.rationale: Eventual consistency with local writes means conflicting writes are only resolved after the fact. Two regions can both 'win' the lock and both submit to an acquirer.
recommendation.verification: Run a game day in which identical keyed requests reach both regions concurrently while replication lag is injected. The acquirer simulator must record exactly one authorization.

findings.statement: New in 1.1: Section 9.4 says a conditional put guarantees exactly one lock holder for a merchant and key, whichever region receives the request. Yet each region writes its own local replica, and replication between them is eventually consistent. A conditional put in Jakarta cannot see an IN_PROGRESS item written in Singapore that has not replicated yet. The scenario the design describes for this table is a merchant retry sent to Jakarta during a partial Singapore outage, while the original may still be running in Singapore. In that case both regions can acquire the lock and both can authorize, which breaks FR-5.
findings.title: Cross-region idempotency lock claim does not hold under eventually consistent global-table replicas

recommendation.expected_benefit: Card acceptance survives the loss of an AZ or HSM, supporting NFR-3 and the RPO/RTO in NFR-4.
recommendation.issue: Every card authorization depends on a single HSM in a single AZ.
recommendation.rationale: Uncached HSM unwraps put the HSM on the synchronous path of every card payment, and the scaling trigger is unreachable at the design load.
recommendation.verification: In a Phase 9 chaos test, terminate the HSM in one AZ at 1,100 card TPS. Card authorizations continue within the NFR-2 budget.

findings.statement: Every detokenise unwraps a DEK inside the HSM with no caching, and the cluster has one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. Losing that AZ or that HSM therefore stops every card authorization and every cascade, because all candidates use the same Vault. That contradicts the three-AZ posture and the NFR-3 target of 99.95%. Card volume at peak is about 55% of 2,000 TPS, roughly 1,100 TPS, so the 1,500 TPS trigger for a second HSM would never fire. Restoring from the daily backup takes a manual rebuild, during which card acceptance is down.
findings.title: A single CloudHSM in one AZ remains a single point of failure for all card payments

Late approvals on non-winning attempts trigger an automatic void, with an exception raised if the void fails. Remove the 'cannot create a duplicate charge' sentence.

findings.statement: A 2,500 ms timeout is classed as retryable, and late responses are discarded. Yet Section 11.2 still says cascading cannot create a duplicate charge because the previous attempt 'did not succeed'. A timed-out attempt may in fact have been approved, in which case the customer holds two authorizations and the first is never recorded or voided. This contradicts P1 and the at-most-one intent of FR-5 and FR-7. During acquirer brownouts, when timeouts cluster, it becomes a volume problem.
findings.title: Cascading after a timeout can leave two authorizations with no reversal path

Attempts in the Aurora lag window are absent after promotion, so they cannot be enumerated for status queries, and the independently replicated idempotency table can reference payments that no longer exist.

next_step.action: Add loss-window injection to the NFR-4 regional game-day script and design the attempt-intent record.

reassessment.note: The relaxed regional RPO and the new NFR-4 test fix the impossible zero-RPO claim. The recovery mechanism that replaces it has the gaps described above.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 20.2, add three things. (1) A durable, cross-region attempt intent record written before acquirer submission, for example in the idempotency global-table item or a replicated attempt log, so that lost attempts can be listed. (2) Use of provider transaction-search or authorization reports (not only settlement files) to find uncaptured authorizations, then void or re-create them. (3) A post-promotion step that reconciles idempotency records against the promoted payment table, re-creates or marks missing payment_ids, and clears orphan IN_PROGRESS locks.
recommendation.expected_benefit: NFR-4 regional recovery becomes achievable and testable, without orphan holds or stuck idempotency keys.
recommendation.issue: The recovery procedure depends on data that the failure it recovers from destroys.
recommendation.rationale: NFR-4's relaxed RPO is acceptable only if the recovery path is actually executable.
recommendation.verification: Run the NFR-4 regional game day with injected Aurora lag of at least 3 s during authorizations. Every lost attempt is listed and resolved, and no key returns a response for a missing payment_id.

findings.statement: NFR-4 now accepts an RPO of up to 5 s, provided every payment in the loss window can be recovered from provider records. Section 20.2 recovers by querying provider status APIs for 'attempts submitted in the last 60 seconds'. But the attempt rows written in that window are the ones lost from Aurora, so the attempts to query cannot be listed. T+1 reconciliation only sees captured and settled lines, so authorized-but-uncaptured holds and wallet payments may never resurface. The DynamoDB replica replicates independently of Aurora, so after promotion it can hold COMPLETED or IN_PROGRESS records for payment_ids that no longer exist. Retries would then return responses for missing payments, or receive 409 with no payment for the sweeper to resolve.
findings.title: Regional loss-window recovery relies on attempt records that are lost in that window

findings.statement: Section 18.4 now requires a two-person rule with a different Owner and step-up MFA, a 48-hour cooling-off period with notice to all Owners and Admins, and validation of the account name against the merchant's legal name. Section 18.3 makes MFA mandatory for every user. Together these close the single-phished-credential path to redirecting payouts, and align with P9 and FR-13.
findings.title: Payout bank account change controls now protect against account takeover

findings.no_change_rationale: A high-cardinality key and WCU-based sizing remove the hot-partition risk for NFR-1. The remaining cross-region concern is covered in FND-002.

reassessment.note: The key schema, LSI removal and WCU arithmetic were corrected in 1.1.

findings.statement: The table now uses the composite key merchant_id#idempotency_key with no LSI, and sizes writes in WCU per KB (up to 6 per request, 12,000 table-wide) with warm throughput set ahead of campaign events. This spreads M-0001's roughly 900 TPS across many partitions, supporting NFR-1 and FR-5 at peak. The provisioning plan should also cover replicated writes on the Jakarta replica.
findings.title: DynamoDB idempotency key and capacity sizing now spread the largest merchant's load

doc_anchors.quote: Each endpoint has a cap of 20 in-flight deliveries and its own circuit breaker, so a failing endpoint cannot starve other merchants.

sound_areas.why_sound: Per-endpoint in-flight caps and circuit breakers, delivery pinned to the validated address with SSRF protection, timestamped HMAC signatures, and bounded retry with a DLQ and replay together meet FR-12 and protect internal services.

doc_anchors.quote: Journals are written in the same PostgreSQL transaction as the payment state transition that causes them, together with an outbox row.

sound_areas.why_sound: The state transition, journal and outbox are written in one transaction, UPDATE and DELETE are revoked on journal and posting, and balances are an asynchronous projection with nightly recomputation that freezes payouts on a mismatch. This serves FR-10, P1, P5 and P7, and avoids hot rows at 2,000 TPS.

doc_anchors.quote: write actions (manual refunds, payout holds, merchant suspension) require just-in-time elevation approved by a second staff member

sound_areas.why_sound: Back-office access requires SSO with hardware MFA and just-in-time elevation approved by a second person, and audit records are written to S3 under compliance-mode Object Lock. This meets P9, P10, FR-16 and NFR-12.
